Giri, ‘mountain’ or ‘height,’ is a word that occurs repeatedly
in the Rigveda.^1 Thus reference is made to the trees on the
hills, hence called ‘tree-haired’ (vṛkṣa-keśāḥ),^2 and to the
streams proceeding from the hills to the sea (samudra).^3 The
term is frequently coupled with the adjectival parvata.^4 The
Rigveda mentions the waters from the hills,^5 and the Athar-
vaveda^6 refers to the snowy mountains. Actual names of
mountains, as Mūjavant, Trikakud, Himavant, are very rare.
References to Krauñca, Mahāmeru, and Maināga, are confined
to the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, while Nāvaprabhraṃśana can no
longer be considered a proper name.^7

Giri-kṣit Auccā-manyava, ‘descendant of Uccāmanyu,’ is
mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (x. 5, 7) as a con-
temporary of Abhipratārin Kākṣaseṇi

Giri-ja Bābhravya, ‘descendant of Babhru,’ is mentioned in
the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (vii. 1) as having been taught by
Śrauta the method of dividing the sacrificial animal (paśor
vibhakti).
